quotes.quote: The optic tracts consist of the axons originating from the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in the retina.

The optic chiasm is an area of partial decussation, in which primarily the nasal retinal fibers traveling through the left and right optic nerves decussate to the contralateral optic chiasm and optic tract.
It has been shown that around 53% of the total optic nerve fibers cross at the optic chiasma, and 47% of the optic nerve fibers do not cross.
By crossing at the optic chiasm, all fibers recording the left visual field of both eyes project to the right hemisphere, and the same applies to the right visual field.
Each optic tract carries one-half of the visual field, consisting of afferent (sensory) information from temporal hemi-retinal fibers ipsilaterally and nasal hemi-retinal fibers contralaterally.

Parvocellular (P) and magnocellular (M) cells of the LGN separate into six layers, in which fibers originating from ipsilateral RGCs synapse onto layers 2, 3, and 5, while contralateral neural information synapses onto layers 1, 4, and 6.

The left and right LGN serve as points of neural origin for optic radiations (Meyer’s loop, central bundle, and Baum’s loop) that travel to the primary visual striate cortex (V1) and several extrastriate locations of the cortex, primarily through the internal capsule.

it is now well established that the four dorsal layers (parvocellular) of the dLGN receive signals about form and color from X-type ganglion cells and the two ventral layers (magnocellular), receive signals about movement from Y-type ganglion cells.
Ventral to each of the magno- and parvocellular layers lie the koniocellular layers, which contain a heterogenous group of neurons whose functions remain to be fully determined.
The inferior radiation first courses anteriorly, along the roof of the lateral ventricle's temporal horn, before turning laterally and projecting through the temporal lobe as a Meyer loop.
The superior pathway courses posteriorly through the parietal lobe before contacting the visual cortex.
The superior bank of the calcarine sulcus receives visual data from the inferior fields, and the inferior bank is responsible for the superior visual field.

The LGN contains an array of axons distributed in 6 laminae or layers that receive the signal from either the ipsilateral or contralateral eye. Such a retinotopic organization is crucial to properly merge binocular images at the occipital cortex.

Simultaneously, some fibers from the optic tract also communicate with the superior colliculus, pretectal nuclei, and suprachiasmatic nuclei, which are involved in multiple physiologic functions, including the light reflex.
Moreover, pulvinar is considered to play an important role in unconscious vision or blindsight
A lesion of the optic nerve anterior to the optic chiasm produces vision loss in the ipsilateral eye.

Lesions of the optic chiasm result in bitemporal hemianopia. The most common causes are pituitary tumors, given the close relationship of the chiasm to the pituitary gland, and aneurysms of the anterior communicating artery.

For instance, right-sided Meyer loop (inferior radiation) damage would cause vision loss in the superior-left quadrant bilaterally (pie in the sky).
The damage to the right optic radiation passing through the parietal lobe causes vision loss in the inferior left quadrant bilaterally (pie on the floor defect).

Bipolar neurons of the Scarpa ganglion convey afferent signals from the otolith organs and semicircular canals through cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) to the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction.
These fibers synapse in the 4 vestibular nuclei—superior, medial, lateral, and inferior—or project directly to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle (juxtarestiform body).
The vestibulocerebellum, comprising the flocculonodular lobe and adjacent vermis, maintains an exclusive functional connection with the vestibular system.
This region receives primary afferent input directly from the Scarpa ganglion and secondary projections from the vestibular nuclei through the juxtarestiform body of the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
The LVST originates from the lateral vestibular nucleus and descends ipsilaterally through the anterior spinal cord to all levels, facilitating activation of extensor muscles in the limbs and trunk.
The MVST arises from the medial vestibular nucleus and travels bilaterally via the MLF, projecting primarily to cervical spinal levels.

Activation of the superior and medial vestibular nuclei during head rotation generates impulses that cross to the contralateral abducens nucleus, stimulating the lateral rectus muscle, while interneuronal projections via the MLF activate the ipsilateral oculomotor nucleus to contract the medial rectus.

The thalamus functions as a central relay for vestibular processing, receiving bilateral input from the superior vestibular nuclei and contralateral projections from the medial vestibular nucleus via the MLF and central tegmental tracts.

Within the thalamus, vestibular signals are primarily processed in the ventral posterior complex, which comprises the ventral posterolateral, ventral posteromedial, and ventral posteroinferior nuclei.
These nuclei integrate vestibular, proprioceptive, and visual inputs and transmit efferent fibers through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the primary somatosensory cortex.
Vestibular input relayed through the thalamus is transmitted to higher-order cortical centers, most prominently converging in the parieto-insular vestibular cortex.
OP2 is a core region within the human cortical vestibular network on the basis of its location

Lesions involving these regions, particularly within the flocculonodular lobe, produce gaze-holding deficits, disrupted smooth tracking, nystagmus, and truncal ataxia, often presenting as a broad-based or “drunken” gait.
The characteristic manifestation of internuclear ophthalmoplegia is impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye, accompanied by abducting nystagmus of the contralateral eye during horizontal gaze.
Damage to the LVST compromises postural control, producing truncal instability, falls, or lateropulsion.
OP2 is homologous to the nonhuman primate parieto-insular vestibular cortex (PIVC)—a “core” cortical vestibular region
It seems that the vestibular cortex has the form of an extensive network rather than a discrete, limited, and well-demarcated cortical location.
Its central processes enter the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction and travel caudally to the medulla oblongata, where they synapse at the nucleus solitarius.
Specifically, the synapse occurs in the rostral part of the nucleus solitarius, known as the gustatory region of the nucleus.
Next, the second-order fibers ascend ipsilaterally to the parvicellular division of the ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPMpc) of the thalamus, where the next synapse occurs.

The third-order fibers travel ipsilaterally through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to terminate in the frontal operculum, anterior insular cortex, and in the rostral part of the Brodmann area 3B.
Additionally, secondary fibers travel from the gustatory cortex to the posterolateral portion of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).

A vestibular schwannoma (also referred to as an acoustic neuroma), which is a benign tumor that grows into the cerebellopontine angle (CPA), can cause loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the ipsilateral side.

The third-order fibers travel ipsilaterally through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to terminate in the frontal operculum, anterior insular cortex, and in the rostral part of the Brodmann area 3B.

Axons from the rostral gustatory solitary nucleus project to the ventral posterior medial nucleus of the thalamus VPM and ultimately terminate, both crossed and uncrossed, at the neocortex, the gustatory cortex (the anterior insula of the temporal lobe and frontal opercular region).
Axonal projections of olfactory nerves synapse with the dendrites of mitral and tufted cells in spherical structures known as glomeruli.

Second-order mitral cells then project via olfactory tracts to specific areas within the brain that process olfactory information, including the piriform cortex, olfactory tubercle, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex.
